Chapter 7: Filters and Reducers

This chapter focuses on pipeline shaping by introducing one filter and three reducers. The service refines incoming candidates after Resolve and derives display-ready values before the UI renders the committed State.

The service registers the filter and reducers, and the component renders the committed display-ready State. That separation makes it clear why filtering, sorting, and display derivation belong in the pipeline instead of inside the template.

Centralize cross-view data rules once.

Filtering, sorting, labels, and derived display values often begin as small template decisions and gradually diverge across screens. This chapter moves those rules into the pipeline, where a candidate collection can be refined once and its display-ready State can be reused by every consumer.

Why this boundary matters

Filters shape the candidate before reducers derive the committed value; neither stage belongs in a component template. Pure, service-registered functions keep the transformation order explicit, prevent repeated view logic, and let each consumer render the same refined and derived State.

Use this structure for

  • removing ineligible or incomplete records before they are rendered
  • sorting collections consistently across multiple views
  • deriving labels and display fields once for every consumer

By the end of this chapter

You will have a pure filter that refines candidate characters and ordered reducers that derive sorting, labels, and full names before the committed State reaches the component.

Chapter 7 Starting Point and Stage Map

Start with a fresh completed Chapter 5 checkpoint, not the FeatureCell instance you destroyed while testing. This chapter changes the character shape/domain helpers, service, component, template, and their specs.

Candidate Progression
  1. Resolve produces the incoming character collection.
  2. The filter removes records that fail this lab's eligibility rule.
  3. The first reducer derives a Force-sensitive display label.
  4. The second reducer clones and sorts by last name.
  5. The third reducer derives the reusable full name.
  6. Only the final display-ready collection becomes committed State.
Teaching Predicate, Not a Universal Domain Rule

Removing the literal last name unknown makes the Filter stage easy to see; it is not a recommendation to discard incomplete people or records. Production filters should encode a defensible rule such as authorization, active status, or validated eligibility. Preserve raw data elsewhere when the application must correct or audit it.

Step 1: Add the Filter Stage
↑ top

This chapter focuses on pipeline shaping. The service still owns the same , but now the incoming candidate collection is refined after the Resolve stage and before any reducer derives the final committed value.

That execution order matters. The filter stage runs after Resolve and before Reducers, so the candidate collection is refined before any reducer logic runs.

In this example, the pure removeUnknownLastNameFilter removes any candidate character whose last name is exactly unknown, so the collection is cleaned before reducer logic derives any display fields.

Make the Change
  1. Open example.filter.ts and add the pure filter that removes characters whose last name is unknown. @for (file of filterFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  2. Open example.service.ts and register that filter with this.#vault.filters(). @for (file of serviceFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
What to Look For
  • The filter runs on the candidate collection produced after Resolve, not on the currently rendered template state.
  • The filter is pure and side-effect free: it returns a refined array and does not mutate the incoming candidate.
  • The service still owns pipeline registration. The component does not decide which characters are filtered.
  • Filter registration order is deterministic, so the reducer stage only sees the already-filtered candidate collection.
  • The seed file contains five characters. Chewbacca has the last name unknown, so this teaching filter removes that record and passes four candidates to the reducers.
Step 2: Register Ordered Reducers
↑ top

After the filter stage refines the candidate collection, reducers derive the display-ready state that the component will actually render. Here, you apply three reducer styles to the same post-filter candidate while keeping the same service-owned boundary.

The order is intentional and matches the pipeline documentation: reducers run after filters.

The first reducer delegates to a pure helper that derives forceSensitiveDisplay.

The second uses a factory function, withCharactersSortedByLastName(), to return a configured reducer.

The third delegates again to deriveFullName so the committed snapshot carries a display-ready full name without pushing string composition into the template.

Why Compose Three Reducers?

Each pure reducer protects one independently testable rule and can be reused without copying template logic. Combine reducers when their operations are inseparable or measured collection size makes repeated passes materially expensive; do not combine them merely to shorten the registration list.

Make the Change
  1. Open example.character-domain.ts and use the existing reducer helpers for force-sensitive (deriveForceSensitiveDisplay) labels, last-name sorting (withCharactersSortedByLastName), and full-name (deriveFullName) derivation. @for (file of characterDomain(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  2. Register those reducers in example.service.ts in the exact order they should run. @for (file of serviceFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
Reducer Styles in This Chapter
  • Reducer 1 is a direct pure reducer helper: deriveForceSensitiveDisplay maps every character to a display-ready Yes or No label.
  • Reducer 2 is a factory-generated reducer: withCharactersSortedByLastName() returns a ReducerFunction that clones and sorts the collection immutably.
  • Reducer 3 is another direct pure reducer helper: deriveFullName derives the final display label that every view reuses.
  • Because reducers run after filters, each reducer works on the already refined candidate collection instead of repeating filter logic.
Trace Chewbacca and Leia Through the Pipeline
  1. Resolve supplies five seed characters. Chewbacca enters with lastName: 'unknown'; Leia enters with lastName: 'Organa'.
  2. removeUnknownLastNameFilter returns a new four-record array. Chewbacca is absent, while Leia continues.
  3. deriveForceSensitiveDisplay adds Leia's forceSensitiveDisplay value.
  4. withCharactersSortedByLastName() clones and sorts the four records into this exact order: Obi-Wan Kenobi, Leia Organa, Luke Skywalker, and Darth Vader.
  5. deriveFullName adds fullName: 'Leia Organa'; that four-record, display-ready collection is committed.
Keep Pipeline Transforms Deterministic

Filters and reducers should be deterministic and side-effect-free for a given candidate. Do not fetch data, write storage, or trigger telemetry from these transforms. Route I/O and recoverable transport work through an explicit service or Resolve boundary before applying domain shaping.

Supporting Domain File

The example.character-domain.ts maintains the draft type, next-ID helper, and character factory used by this add/edit slice.

This file is intentionally separate so the service stays minimal and the chapter stays focused on the state boundary instead of helper logic.

Step 3: Update the Component and HTML
↑ top

The filters and reducers chapter is complete once the page no longer composes display values in the template, the reducer-derived character fields drive the visible UI, and the filter and reducer source appears in text areas for direct comparison.

That is the key architectural result of this chapter. The component still owns selection, editor, and feedback state, but it now renders a collection that has already moved through Resolve, Filter, and Reducer stages. The template reads fullName and forceSensitiveDisplay directly instead of concatenating names or translating booleans inline, which keeps display rules inside the pipeline rather than scattered across markup.

Make the Change
  1. Update example.component.ts to keep the same component/service boundary while exposing the filter and reducer source views. @for (file of componentFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
  2. Update example.component.html so the details panel reads reducer-derived fields and the page shows filter and reducer source text areas. @for (file of htmlFiles(); track file?.type) { 
    {{ file?.source }}
     }
What to Look for
  • The filter passes four eligible records to three ordered, immutable reducers.
  • The template consumes sorted and derived committed fields instead of recreating rules.
  • Save this checkpoint for Chapter 8, which turns one filter into a controlled failure source.
Step 4: Chapter Round-up
↑ top

The Filters and Reducers chapter is complete once the application is running and can confirm the characters are successfully filtered and reduced.

Run and Verify
  1. Verify that the displayed source views and reducer-driven UI values match the committed state.
  2. Confirm Chewbacca is absent, the four remaining records are sorted by last name, and every visible record contains the two derived display fields. Verify the helpers return new arrays rather than mutating their inputs.
Chapter 7 Summary
  • The template now renders reducer-derived fullName and forceSensitiveDisplay instead of computing those values inline.
  • The page now includes dedicated text areas that surface the filter and each reducer source for direct comparison.
  • The service now demonstrates pipeline-stage registration, not just CRUD mutations, while preserving the same service-owned boundary.
